Paths and display logic

Source: vignettes/paths-and-display-logic.Rmd
paths-and-display-logic.Rmd

What this answers. How the paths through a survey are reconstructed, and what the structural profile’s weights mean.

What you need. A .qsf.

What to keep in mind. The structural profile weights the survey’s design, and response data gives the distribution across respondents. The package treats each branch condition on its own, so the profile’s extremes may come from routes whose conditions contradict each other.

This article covers how surveyBurden reconstructs the paths through a survey and turns them into a burden spread. It also explains how the structural profile differs from respondent burden. For per-question scoring see vignette("gfs-scoring"), and for the printed output see vignette("reading-the-report").

library(surveyBurden)
#> 
#>                   .-- Q2 -- Q3 --.
#>   survey -- Q1 --+               +-- Burden 0.3.0
#>                   '-- Q4 --------'
#> 
#> An R package for assessing the response-burden of web surveys
#> Docs: https://pmpk20.github.io/surveyBurden/
#> 
#> Please cite: King P (2026). surveyBurden: An R package for assessing
#> the response-burden of web surveys. R package version 0.3.0,
#> https://github.com/pmpk20/surveyBurden.
#> Use citation("surveyBurden") for BibTeX.
demo <- system.file("extdata", "demo_travel_survey.qsf", package = "surveyBurden")
qsf <- read_qsf(demo)
report <- burden_report(demo, quiet = TRUE)

Survey flow

Modern web surveys route respondents through different sequences of blocks. resolve_flow() walks the SurveyFlow. At every Branch it forks into a continuation where the condition holds and one where it fails, and at every EndSurvey it forks into a screen-out. Most branch conditions depend on embedded data or earlier answers that only fieldwork reveals, so both outcomes are kept.

Branches that compare one embedded field with a value (=, !=, >, >=, <, <=) are handled differently. The field holds one value along a path, so every branch on it agrees with that value, and a fixed value set earlier in the flow (including one a randomiser picks) decides the branch. A run of equality tests on one field (“group is 1”, “group is 2”, …) becomes one path per value plus a “none matches” path, because the field could hold any value. When you know the values a field can hold, declare them.

burden_report(qsf, field_domains = list(group = c("1", "2")))

The package then keeps the “none matches” path only when a declared value matches no branch. The result is every block sequence a respondent could encounter.

resolve_flow(qsf)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   path_id block_ids  terminates_early decisions
#>     <int> <list>     <lgl>            <list>   
#> 1       1 <chr [2]>  TRUE             <lgl [1]>
#> 2       2 <chr [3]>  TRUE             <lgl [2]>
#> 3       3 <chr [12]> FALSE            <lgl [3]>
#> 4       4 <chr [11]> FALSE            <lgl [3]>
nrow(report$paths)
#> [1] 4
sum(report$paths$status == "complete")
#> [1] 2
sum(report$paths$status == "screen_out")
#> [1] 2

A block randomiser that shows m of its M elements (“present 1 of 3 blocks”) becomes one path per combination of elements, each in survey order, because order leaves burden unchanged. With even presentation each combination is equally likely, which matches the equal weight each path gets. When the number shown is unreadable, every element is treated as shown, with a warning. A randomiser holding only embedded-data assignments shows no blocks itself. It adds paths only when a later branch tests a field it sets (one path per value it can assign). The package enumerates paths up to max_paths (10000), and a flow that would produce more raises an error instead of returning a partial answer.

Display logic

Within a path, resolve_paths() splits the questions into three sets.

  • Always shown.
  • May be shown, gated by a condition that depends on fieldwork.
  • Never shown on this path, because the gate’s trigger question is absent from this path.
rp <- resolve_paths(qsf)
data.frame(
  path_id    = rp$path_id,
  screen_out = rp$terminates_early,
  n_always   = lengths(rp$q_always),
  n_maybe    = lengths(rp$q_maybe),
  n_gates    = rp$n_gates
)
#>   path_id screen_out n_always n_maybe n_gates
#> 1       1       TRUE        2       0       0
#> 2       2       TRUE        3       0       0
#> 3       3      FALSE       20       6       4
#> 4       4      FALSE       20       3       3

Qualtrics stores display logic as If / ElseIf / AndIf groups. The package folds each group left to right. It combines ElseIf clauses with OR and AndIf clauses with AND, and treats a missing type as AND. Keeping the OR clauses matters, because a question can appear when any one of several conditions holds.

Path enumeration

path_burden_profile() works inside the “may be shown” set and enumerates the display-logic states the package can model.

  • Conditional questions are grouped into coupling components. Two questions couple if they share a gate, directly or through a chain of shared gates.
  • A component with at most max_condition_states (default 10000) joint gate states is enumerated in full. Every joint state of its gates that the model represents is included, respecting single-choice mutual exclusion and conditions joined by AND across gates. A stored (embedded data) field compared with EqualTo, NotEqualTo or an inequality is enumerated over its distinguishable values, so conditions on different values of one field are mutually exclusive. “In full” means exhaustive within the model. A field compared with any other operator is treated as a free true/false condition, and branch conditions and display logic are enumerated separately.
  • A larger component (dozens of questions keyed off one popular trigger such as employment status) uses a primary-gate approximation. Each question is scored against its first gate, and its other gates are treated as passed.
  • Separate components are combined as independent.
  • Loop & Merge blocks are unrolled to the explicit ?v=N cap. The structural profile treats the iteration count as uniform over 1 to N, unless loop_weights gives other weights (for example loop_weights = list(BL_x = c(1, 1, 1, 9))).
  • Display logic inside a loop is evaluated. A trigger in the same loop block is answered afresh in each iteration. A trigger outside the block (an earlier question or a stored field) has one answer for every iteration, shared with any question outside the loop that uses it. A “Loop 1 … Current Loop” condition holds in the first iteration only.
  • A hidden trigger question stays unanswered, so every question it gates stays hidden too. A shown trigger with a forced response is always answered (respect_force_response = TRUE, the default).
pbp <- path_burden_profile(qsf)
pbp[, c("path_id", "terminates_early", "burden_min",
        "burden_median", "burden_max")]
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   path_id terminates_early burden_min burden_median burden_max
#>     <int> <lgl>                 <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1       1 TRUE                     12            12         12
#> 2       2 TRUE                     14            14         14
#> 3       3 FALSE                   103           121        143
#> 4       4 FALSE                   103           119        139
nrow(pbp$profile[[3]])   # distinct modelled burden values on complete path 3
#> [1] 41

Each row of a profile table is one modelled burden value with a structural weight. Each joint gate state and each loop iteration count gets equal weight, a value produced by several states carries their combined weight, and the weights on a path sum to 1. That weight comes from the model of the design. Respondent shares come from response data.

Burden by block for each traversal

path_burden_traversals() returns the traversals behind the profile, with one row per traversal and block giving points, items, response items and pages. A cumulative-by-block curve and the totals therefore come from the same weighted traversals. Small surveys are enumerated exactly, and larger ones are sampled with a fixed seed (traversal_stability() reports the spread across seeds). field_rules can derive stored fields that survey code computes and the survey file leaves out.

tr <- path_burden_traversals(qsf, method = "exact")
head(tr[, c("traversal_id", "path_id", "weight", "block_id", "points")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   traversal_id path_id  weight block_id points
#>          <int>   <int>   <dbl> <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1            1       3 0.00139 BL1          11
#> 2            1       3 0.00139 BL2           1
#> 3            1       3 0.00139 BL3           2
#> 4            1       3 0.00139 BL4          15
#> 5            1       3 0.00139 BL5           3
#> 6            1       3 0.00139 BL6           4

Structural and respondent burden

This distinction is central, and it is easy to state wrongly.

The default result is a structural burden profile. It covers the combinations of optional questions the package can model, weighted by the model. Each complete path carries equal total weight, and within a path each modelled combination does. When the report says the median is 120 points, it means the median of that model-weighted distribution. How common each path or combination is among respondents is a separate question, which only response data can answer.

For a distribution across respondents, supply response data. burden_report(qsf, responses = ...) adds $respondents, the quantiles and mean of respondent burden over complete responses. Each respondent counts once, so paths taken by more respondents carry more weight. See vignette("respondent-burden") for the measure and the data it needs.
